prompt.content: You are AEGIS, an expert embedded systems AI assistant specialized in MCU architecture selection, firmware code generation, and hardware/firmware debugging across STM32, ESP32, PIC, AVR, and RTOS-based embedded platforms.
Why is STM32 used instead of ESP32 for the main flight controller in a drone?

chosen.content: STM32 is chosen for the primary flight-stabilization role mainly because of its hardware FPU (on F4/F7/H7 parts) and deterministic, low-jitter interrupt handling via the NVIC — both critical for running PID control loops and sensor fusion at multi-kHz rates with bounded latency. It also exposes more DMA-capable UART/SPI/I2C peripherals, needed to talk to GPS, IMU, compass, receiver, and ESCs simultaneously without blocking the CPU. ESP32 is excellent for wireless companion tasks (Wi-Fi/BLE telemetry, FPV video) but its dual-core RTOS scheduling isn't built for hard-real-time determinism, which is why it's used alongside an STM32 FC rather than in place of it.

rejected.content: ESP32 just isn't as good a chip as STM32 for drones because STM32 is more powerful and has more features overall, so it's better at everything including flight control. ESP32 is mainly used for Wi-Fi so it's not as fast. STM32 also has more memory usually, which helps it fly the drone better.

prompt.content: You are AEGIS, an expert embedded systems AI assistant specialized in MCU architecture selection, firmware code generation, and hardware/firmware debugging across STM32, ESP32, PIC, AVR, and RTOS-based embedded platforms.
Explain what makes STM32F7 better than STM32F4 for a flight controller.

chosen.content: F7 (Cortex-M7) offers a higher clock speed (up to ~216MHz vs F4's ~168-180MHz) and typically more RAM/flash plus a data cache, which gives real headroom for heavier real-time DSP — more aggressive dynamic notch filtering on gyro data, higher PID looptimes, and richer blackbox logging without starving the control loop. Both F4 and F7 have a hardware FPU, so the core stabilization math works fine on either; the difference is how much *additional* filtering/logging/feature load the chip can absorb before it starts competing with the control loop for cycles.

rejected.content: F7 is better than F4 because it has a floating point unit that F4 doesn't have, which lets it do the math needed for gyro and PID calculations. Without an FPU, F4 boards can't really run Betaflight properly and have to do everything in slow integer math, which is why F7 boards are the only real option for serious flight control.

prompt.content: You are AEGIS, an expert embedded systems AI assistant specialized in MCU architecture selection, firmware code generation, and hardware/firmware debugging across STM32, ESP32, PIC, AVR, and RTOS-based embedded platforms.
What does the PIC MCU do on a drone ESC, and what protocol talks to it?

chosen.content: PIC (typically PIC16/PIC18, or Silicon Labs 32-bit variants on higher-end ESCs) runs firmware such as BLHeli_32 directly on the ESC board, converting a commanded throttle value into precisely timed 3-phase commutation signals for the brushless motor. It communicates with the flight controller over DShot, a digital protocol that transmits discrete throttle values with a checksum and supports bidirectional telemetry (RPM, voltage, current) back to the FC — this is a separate real-time problem from flight stabilization, handled on separate silicon per motor.

rejected.content: The PIC chip is basically a smaller version of the STM32 flight controller that sits on the ESC and helps it process the flight data faster. It uses the same DShot protocol as the main flight controller uses for GPS and telemetry, which is why DShot is called a universal drone protocol. Since PIC is less powerful than STM32, it usually needs the FC to do most of the actual motor timing calculations for it.

prompt.content: You are AEGIS, an expert embedded systems AI assistant specialized in MCU architecture selection, firmware code generation, and hardware/firmware debugging across STM32, ESP32, PIC, AVR, and RTOS-based embedded platforms.
Why does the Pixhawk 4 use two separate STM32 chips instead of one?

chosen.content: Pixhawk 4 splits the workload across an STM32F765 running the full autopilot stack (sensor fusion, navigation, control loops, logging) and a smaller STM32F100 acting as an independent failsafe/IO co-processor for RC input and direct motor/servo output. The separation exists so that a software fault, hang, or firmware-update failure on the complex main MCU can't take down the aircraft — the simpler, more thoroughly verified failsafe chip can maintain minimal safe control independently, the same principle used in safety-critical automotive and avionics architectures.

rejected.content: Two chips are used mainly for performance — running the flight code on two separate STM32s lets Pixhawk 4 split the PID loop calculations in half so each chip only has to do half the math, roughly doubling the maximum control loop frequency compared to a single-chip design. The F100 is a smaller chip that just does the leftover calculations the F765 doesn't have time for.

prompt.content: You are AEGIS, an expert embedded systems AI assistant specialized in MCU architecture selection, firmware code generation, and hardware/firmware debugging across STM32, ESP32, PIC, AVR, and RTOS-based embedded platforms.
Is ATmega/AVR still a reasonable choice for a new flight controller design today?

chosen.content: No, not for primary flight stabilization in a new design. AVR's 8-bit core lacks a hardware FPU, so the floating-point math used in attitude estimation and PID control runs as slow software-emulated float; it also has fewer DMA-capable peripherals than STM32, making it harder to service GPS, IMU, receiver, and ESC I/O simultaneously without blocking the CPU. AVR's role in FC history is real — it powered the original ArduPilotMega — but that's exactly why it's now considered obsolete for this job: the workload has outgrown what an 8-bit core without an FPU can deliver deterministically. If cost is the constraint, a low-end STM32F1/F3 is a better comparison point than AVR.

rejected.content: AVR can still work fine for a flight controller as long as the firmware is optimized well, since 8-bit vs 32-bit mostly just affects how the code is compiled rather than actual real-time performance. Modern AVR chips run at high enough clock speeds that the lack of an FPU isn't really a bottleneck anymore, and plenty of hobby drones still use Arduino-based flight controllers successfully today.

My DShot600 signal desyncs motors at high throttle but DShot300 works fine on the same STM32F405 board. What's the most likely root cause to check first?

chosen.content: This "works at the lower bitrate, fails at the higher one under load" pattern points at timing margin rather than protocol logic. Start by checking DMA channel/priority conflicts — DShot600's ~1.67us bit period leaves little slack, so if the DMA stream driving motor PWM shares a controller with another high-traffic peripheral (e.g., high-rate gyro SPI), a priority inversion under load can delay the DShot burst just enough to blur bit timing. Also verify the actual APB timer clock matches what your prescaler assumes — a clock-tree mismatch shifts high-time proportionally, tolerable at DShot300's looser window but not at DShot600's tighter one.

rejected.content: This is almost always a power supply issue — DShot600 needs more current to run at the higher signaling rate, so at high throttle the extra current draw from the motors causes a brownout on the signal line itself, corrupting the bits. The fix is usually to add a larger capacitor near the ESC connector to smooth out the DShot600 signal voltage, since DShot300 draws less current and doesn't trigger the same brownout.

prompt.content: You are AEGIS, an expert embedded systems AI assistant specialized in MCU architecture selection, firmware code generation, and hardware/firmware debugging across STM32, ESP32, PIC, AVR, and RTOS-based embedded platforms.
Compare Holybro Kakute F7 and Matek F405 for a freestyle FPV build in terms of MCU capability.

chosen.content: Both use STM32 with a hardware FPU, so core stabilization performs well on either. The practical difference is headroom: Kakute F7 (Cortex-M7, more RAM, higher clock) has more margin for multiple dynamic notch filters, higher PID looptimes, and high-rate blackbox logging without dropping frames. Matek F405 (Cortex-M4) handles standard Betaflight stabilization fine but has less margin — at very aggressive filtering combined with very high looptimes, firmware may need to trade off filter complexity or looptime to stay real-time. For a typical freestyle build with moderate filtering needs, F405 is sufficient and cheaper; F7 is worth it if you're pushing high looptimes with heavy filtering or plan to add compute-heavy features.

rejected.content: Kakute F7 is strictly better in every way and Matek F405 should only be used as a budget option with reduced performance, since F405 lacks a proper floating point unit and can't run true PID calculations — it uses a simplified fixed-point approximation instead, which is why F7 boards are generally required for competitive freestyle flying and F405 is mainly aimed at beginners.

prompt.content: You are AEGIS, an expert embedded systems AI assistant specialized in MCU architecture selection, firmware code generation, and hardware/firmware debugging across STM32, ESP32, PIC, AVR, and RTOS-based embedded platforms.
What's the actual difference between PWM and DShot for controlling ESCs, from a protocol design standpoint?

chosen.content: PWM is an analog, duty-cycle-encoded protocol — throttle is represented by pulse width within a fixed period, with no error checking, so any noise on the line silently becomes a (possibly wrong) throttle value. DShot is a digital protocol: it sends an 11-bit throttle value plus a telemetry-request bit and a 4-bit checksum in a fixed 16-bit frame, so the ESC can detect and reject a corrupted frame rather than acting on it, and (with bidirectional DShot) return telemetry like RPM, voltage, and current to the flight controller over the same line. The tradeoff is that DShot requires precise timer-driven bit timing on both ends rather than a simple duty-cycle measurement, which is why it typically needs a hardware timer + DMA rather than being bit-banged.

rejected.content: DShot is just a faster version of PWM — it uses the exact same duty-cycle encoding but at a higher frequency, which is why it's named by its speed (DShot300 = 300Hz, DShot600 = 600Hz, etc., versus standard PWM at 50Hz). The main benefit is just reduced latency from the higher update rate; there's no real structural difference in how the signal is encoded or interpreted by the ESC.

What are the process noise and measurement noise values used in the kalman1D function?

chosen.content: In kalman1D, the process noise term is 16 (uncertainty += dt * dt * 16), and the measurement noise term is 9, used as kalmanGain = uncertainty / (uncertainty + 9).
